content: During controlled clinical trials in the United States, 521 patients with vulvovaginal candidiasis were treated with TERAZOL® 7 (terconazole) 0.4% vaginal cream. The adverse reactions most likely associated with the use of this cream, based on comparisons with placebo, included headache (26% in the terconazole group versus 17% in the placebo group) and body pain (2.1% versus 0% with placebo). Vulvovaginal burning (5.2%), itching (2.3%), and irritation (3.1%) were reported less frequently with terconazole 0.4% vaginal cream compared to the placebo. Fever (1.7% versus 0.5% with placebo) and chills (0.4% versus 0% with placebo) were also reported. The rate of therapy-related discontinuation was 1.9%, with vulvovaginal itching being the most common reason for discontinuation (0.6% in the terconazole group versus 0.9% in the placebo group). In another set of controlled clinical trials conducted in the United States, patients with vulvovaginal candidiasis were treated with TERAZOL® 3 (terconazole) 0.8% vaginal cream for three days. The adverse reactions most likely related to this treatment included headache (21% in the terconazole group versus 16% in the placebo group) and dysmenorrhea (6% versus 2% with placebo). General genital complaints, including burning and itching, were less frequent with the terconazole 0.8% vaginal cream three-day regimen (5% versus 6%–9% with placebo). Other reported adverse reactions included abdominal pain (3.4% versus 1% with placebo) and fever (1% versus 0.3% with placebo). The therapy-related discontinuation rate was 2.0%, with vulvovaginal itching being the most common reason for discontinuation (0.7% in the terconazole group versus 0.3% in the placebo group). In a separate study involving TERAZOL® 3 (terconazole) 80 mg vaginal suppositories, 284 patients with vulvovaginal candidiasis were treated, and their outcomes were compared to 295 patients receiving placebo. The adverse reactions most likely related to the suppositories included headache (30.3% in the terconazole group versus 20.7% in the placebo group) and pain in the female genitalia (4.2% versus 0.7% with placebo). Burning (15.2% versus 11.2% with placebo) and body pain (3.9% versus 1.7% with placebo) were also reported, though these differences were not statistically significant. Fever (2.8% versus 1.4% with placebo) and chills (1.8% versus 0.7% with placebo) were additional reported adverse reactions. The therapy-related discontinuation rate was 3.5% in the terconazole group compared to 2.7% in the placebo group. Burning (2.5% versus 1.4% with placebo) and pruritus (1.8% versus 1.4% with placebo) were the most common reasons for discontinuation. Post-marketing surveillance has identified additional adverse reactions associated with TERAZOL®. These include general symptoms such as asthenia and influenza-like illness, which may involve fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, arthralgia, and malaise. Immune system reactions include hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis, and facial edema. Nervous system reactions include dizziness. Respiratory reactions include bronchospasm. Skin-related adverse reactions include rash, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and urticaria.
